title: What is the difference between the Facade pattern (new simple interface over complex subsystems) and the Adapter pattern (make one incompatible interface match another)?
shortTitle: Facade pattern vs Adapter pattern: a simple interface over a subsystem vs making incompatible interfaces match
keyPoints: Facade gives one simple front door to a complex subsystem; Adapter translates one incompatible interface into the one the client expects.
Facade simplifies and unifies many collaborating classes you own; Adapter translates one specific existing interface you cannot change.
Facade lets you design a brand-new convenient interface; Adapter must conform the adaptee to a fixed target interface.
You add a Facade proactively when a subsystem is painful to use; you add an Adapter reactively to bridge a mismatch.
A Facade usually fronts many subsystem classes; an Adapter usually wraps a single adaptee.
They can coexist: a Facade can internally use Adapters to talk to incompatible subsystem pieces.

s1_definition.oneliner: Facade gives one simple front door to a complex subsystem; Adapter translates one incompatible interface into the one the client expects.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Facade** – provides a single, simplified interface over a complex subsystem of many classes, hiding their interactions so clients deal with one easy entry point.
- **Adapter** – converts the interface of an existing class into another interface that a client expects, so two incompatible types can work together.
- **Intent difference** – Facade simplifies and unifies; Adapter translates and bridges.
- **Interface design** – with Facade you create a new convenient interface; with Adapter you conform to a fixed target interface.
- **Trigger** – Facade is proactive simplification; Adapter is reactive glue for a discovered mismatch.
s1_definition.analogy: A Facade is like the single relationship manager at National Bank of India who handles Rajesh's whole request. Behind her are many departments: accounts, loans, cards, compliance. She gives Rajesh one simple door into a complicated building. An Adapter is different: imagine Rajesh brings a foreign credit-score report in a format the bank's loan software cannot read. The bank uses a small translator that converts that report into the exact format the software expects. The Facade simplifies a building; the Adapter makes one specific thing fit a socket.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Facade
  ──────
  Client ──→ AccountOpeningFacade.openAccount()
                    │
          ┌─────────┼─────────┬──────────┐
          ▼         ▼         ▼          ▼
       KycService  Repo   CardIssuer  Notifier

  Adapter
  ───────
  Client ──→ CreditScoreProvider.getScore(pan)
                    │
                    ▼
              CibilAdapter
                    │
                    ▼
              CibilApi.fetch(request)
              (incompatible third-party)
```

```text
  Facade + Adapter together
  ─────────────────────────
  Controller ──→ LoanApprovalFacade.approveLoan()
                       │
            ┌──────────┼──────────┐
            ▼          ▼          ▼
     CibilAdapter   LoanRepo   Notifier
         │
         ▼
     CibilApi (vendor)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Facade pattern and the Adapter pattern are both structural patterns that wrap other objects, which is why they are easily confused, but their intent is completely different. A Facade provides a single simplified interface over a complex subsystem of many classes, hiding their interactions so the client deals with one easy entry point. An Adapter converts the interface of an existing class into a different interface that the client expects, so two incompatible types work together.

The cleanest way to distinguish them is by asking one question: am I simplifying many collaborating classes into one convenient interface, or am I translating one specific thing into a different expected interface? If it is simplification over a subsystem, it is a Facade. If it is translation to achieve compatibility, it is an Adapter. A Facade usually fronts many subsystem classes and lets you design a brand-new convenient interface, while an Adapter typically wraps a single adaptee and must conform to a target interface that already exists.

In the banking project at National Bank of India, the account-opening flow uses both. Opening an account requires KYC, saving the account, issuing a card, and sending a welcome message. Rajesh created an `AccountOpeningFacade` with a single `openAccount` method that orchestrates all four services. That is a Facade. Inside that flow, the credit-score lookup uses a `CibilAdapter` that implements the bank's `CreditScoreProvider` interface and translates calls into the vendor's incompatible API. That is an Adapter. The Facade uses the Adapter internally, showing the patterns are complementary.

A couple of standard Java examples: `Arrays.asList` adapts an array to the `List` interface (Adapter), and SLF4J bindings adapt one logging API to another (Adapter), while any service class wrapping repositories and clients to expose one business operation is a Facade.

Remember one sentence: Facade simplifies a complex building into one front door, Adapter makes one incompatible plug fit a different socket.
